cues.text: Let us turn now to big data and analytics, the fourth chapter of this study session.
We begin with a definition.
Big data describes data workloads whose scale, speed or complexity exceed convenient traditional processing.
Notice what this definition does not say.
It does not name a fixed number of gigabytes or terabytes.
It says the workload goes beyond what traditional tools can process conveniently.
So big data is relative to the tools and methods an organisation already has.
A volume of data that a modern system handles easily might overwhelm a spreadsheet, and that is the key idea.
To make this concrete, practitioners describe big data using five words that all begin with the letter V.
You will see a table in your notes with three columns: the V, its meaning, and an example.
Let us walk through it row by row.
First, Volume.
Its meaning is the amount of data, and the example is millions of transactions.
Think of a bank or a mobile payments provider recording every transfer, every balance check and every card payment, all day, every day.
The sheer quantity is what we mean by volume.
Second, Velocity.
This is the arrival and processing speed of data, and the example is streaming sensor events.
Imagine sensors on a machine or a vehicle sending readings continuously.
The data does not wait politely in a file.
It keeps arriving, and sometimes it must be processed as it arrives.
Third, Variety.
This means different formats, and the example lists tables, JSON, images and text.
Tables are the neat rows and columns we know from databases.
JSON is a flexible text format that applications use to exchange structured data.
Images and free text have no fixed row and column shape at all.
Real organisations hold all of these together, and that mixture is variety.
Fourth, Veracity.
This means reliability and quality, and the example is missing or duplicated readings.
If a sensor skips a reading, or the same transaction is recorded twice, then the data cannot be trusted at face value.
Veracity reminds us that more data is not automatically better data.
Fifth, Value.
This means useful outcomes, and the example is reduced fraud or waste.
This is the most important V from a business point of view.
Data that is collected, stored and processed but never changes a decision has cost money and produced nothing.
Value is the reason the other four Vs are worth managing.
Now, how do these pieces fit together technically?
The source states that big-data architecture connects sources, ingestion, storage, processing, analytics and serving, with governance and security across all stages.
Please hold on to that last clause.
Governance and security are not one box at the end of the chain.
They apply across every stage, from the moment data is captured to the moment a result is delivered.
Your notes include a diagram, and I encourage you to look at it as I describe it, because it reads from top to bottom as a flow.
At the top we have applications, sensors and transactions.
These are the sources.
From there, an arrow leads to batch or event ingestion.
Ingestion means bringing the data into the system, either in batches, which are collected chunks moved at intervals, or as events, which are individual records moved as they happen.
Next, an arrow leads to a data lake or operational stores.
This is where the data is kept.
Then an arrow leads to cleaning and distributed processing.
Here the data is cleaned, and the work is spread across many machines so that large volumes can be handled.
Next, an arrow leads to a warehouse or models.
This is where integrated data is organised for analysis, and where models are built.
Finally, an arrow leads to dashboards, alerts, decisions and feedback.
This is the serving end, where people and systems actually use the results.
Notice the word feedback.
The outcomes of decisions flow back and shape future data and future decisions, so the process is a cycle and not a one-way street.
Next, let us name the main technologies the source mentions.
Hadoop supports distributed storage and batch processing.
Spark supports distributed analytics and streaming workloads.
Kafka transports and stores event streams.
So, in simple terms, Hadoop is associated with storing large data across many machines and processing it in batches.
Spark is used for analytics across many machines, including streaming.
Kafka moves streams of events between systems and can keep them stored.
Then we have the storage concepts.
A data lake retains diverse raw and curated data.
Raw means data kept close to its original form, and curated means data that has been tidied and prepared.
A warehouse organises integrated analytical data, meaning data from different sources brought together in a structured way for analysis.
The difference to remember is that the lake keeps variety, while the warehouse imposes organisation.
Two processing patterns are also named.
ETL stands for extract, transform and load.
You extract data from its sources, transform it into the needed form, and then load it into its destination.
ELT stands for extract, load and transform.
Here you load the data first, and transform it afterwards.
The only difference is the order of the last two steps, but that order has real design consequences.
The source also notes that cloud supports elastic resources.
Elastic means you can scale computing and storage up or down as demand changes.
However, the source is clear that governance, cost and network dependencies remain.
Moving to the cloud does not remove the need to control who may use the data, to watch spending, or to rely on a working network connection.
Now we turn to analytics, which is the work of drawing meaning from data.
The source gives four categories.
Descriptive analytics answers what happened.
Diagnostic analytics answers why it happened.
Predictive analytics answers what is likely to happen.
Prescriptive analytics answers what action is recommended.
The source illustrates all four with a retail example, and please treat it as an illustration, not as a recorded case.
In retail, descriptive reports show declining sales.
That tells us what happened.
Diagnostic analysis identifies stockouts, meaning products were not available on the shelves, and that explains why sales fell.
Predictive analysis forecasts demand, estimating how much customers are likely to want in future.
Prescriptive optimisation recommends replenishment, suggesting what stock to order and when.
Two cautions are given, and they matter.
First, predictive models are uncertain.
A forecast is an estimate, not a promise.
Second, prescriptive recommendations require objectives, constraints and human judgment.

A system can only recommend well if someone has defined what the organisation is trying to achieve and what limits apply, and people remain responsible for deciding whether to follow the recommendation.
Finally, let us look at where all this is applied, and what makes it difficult.
The source lists applications in healthcare monitoring, finance fraud detection, logistics routing, agricultural forecasting, telecom network optimisation, education and manufacturing.
The source gives these as areas of application without detailing specific cases, so we will not invent any.
The challenges it lists are these: incomplete data, biased samples, inconsistent definitions, privacy, storage and processing costs, skills, infrastructure and integration.
Let me connect a few of them back to what we learned.
Incomplete data and biased samples are problems of veracity, because they weaken trust in the results.
Inconsistent definitions arise when different parts of an organisation mean different things by the same term, which makes integration into a warehouse difficult.
Privacy ties back to the governance and security that must run across every stage of the architecture.
And costs, skills, infrastructure and integration remind us that big data is as much an organisational capability as a technical one.
To summarise the chapter in one thread: big data is defined by workloads that outgrow convenient traditional processing, described through volume, velocity, variety, veracity and value.
It is handled through an architecture from sources to serving, with governance and security throughout.
It is turned into insight through descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics, always with awareness of uncertainty, human judgment and the practical challenges that remain.
